holidays.name: National Gazpacho Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the chilled tomato-based soup that proves soup doesn't need to be hot to be wonderful. Perfect for anyone who wants to eat a salad through a straw.
holidays.origin: Gazpacho originated in the Andalusian region of southern Spain, where farmers blended stale bread, garlic, olive oil, and vinegar to stay cool in the heat. Tomatoes and peppers were added after they arrived from the Americas.
holidays.funFact: Early versions of gazpacho were white, not red, because tomatoes hadn't yet arrived in Europe. The white almond-and-garlic soup ajo blanco is considered its ancestor.

holidays.name: National Microwave Oven Day
holidays.description: A salute to the humble box that reheats your leftover pizza and has launched a million exploded potatoes. Celebrate by finally cleaning that splattered ceiling.
holidays.origin: The day honors the birthday of Percy Spencer, the engineer who noticed that a candy bar in his pocket melted while he stood near a magnetron at Raytheon in the 1940s, leading to the invention of the microwave oven.
holidays.funFact: The first commercial microwave oven, the Radarange, stood nearly 6 feet tall, weighed about 750 pounds, and was water-cooled.

holidays.name: St. Nicholas Day
holidays.description: A beloved European tradition where children leave shoes or boots out overnight in hopes of waking to candy, fruit, and small gifts. Be good, or risk getting a lump of coal or a bundle of twigs.
holidays.origin: It honors Saint Nicholas of Myra, a 4th-century bishop famous for secret gift-giving, including the story of him tossing gold coins through a window to save three sisters from hardship. His legend later inspired Santa Claus.
holidays.funFact: In the Netherlands and parts of Central Europe, St. Nicholas is accompanied by sidekicks like Krampus, a horned, chain-rattling beast who punishes naughty children.

holidays.name: Put Candles in the Window Day
holidays.description: A cozy, glowing observance in which people place candles in their windows to welcome travelers, brighten the dark, and add some festive charm to the long winter nights.
holidays.origin: The custom is rooted in Irish tradition, where a candle in the window symbolized welcome to strangers and wandering travelers, and in the Christmas season it came to represent hospitality for Mary and Joseph.
holidays.funFact: In Irish lore, the candle was traditionally lit by the youngest member of the household, and on Christmas Eve it was left burning all night.

holidays.name: Miners' Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the people who dig deep, literally, to supply the materials that power the modern world. Hard hats off, and maybe say thanks to a rock.
holidays.origin: Miners' Day is observed on December 6 in the United States to recognize the 1907 Monongah mine disaster in West Virginia, the worst mining disaster in U.S. history, which killed 362 men and boys.
holidays.funFact: The Monongah disaster helped spur the creation of the U.S. Bureau of Mines in 1910 and major improvements in mine safety laws.
